items.bron: Emory University report (2010) on Armelagos and Nelson, American Journal of Physical Anthropology: Nubian bones from about AD 350-550 hold tetracycline from fermented grain beer, built into the bone over years, so a substance that acts on bacteria in the body was being taken. https://news.emory.edu/emory-report-archive/stories/2010/09/07/beer.html . Also Salvarsan (1910) and the sulfonamides (Prontosil, 1935) acted on bacteria inside the body before penicillin was in wide use. Science History Institute, Gerhard Domagk: https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/gerhard-domagk . The lesson itself says in the last study block that penicillin healed 'waar ouer medisyne misluk het', which assumes older medicine existed.
items.regstelling: The point (there was nothing reliable for most of history) is right, but 'niks' is an absolute, and evidence contradicts it: ancient brews that held an antibiotic, plant remedies, and the first chemical medicines from 1910 and the 1930s. Narrow the quantifier, do not cut the sentence. For example: for most of history there was no medicine that could reliably kill bacteria inside the body or stop them growing. That also agrees with 'ouer medisyne' later in the lesson.

items.bron: The qualifiers hold up against the earlier candidates. Pyocyanase (Emmerich and Löw, 1899) came from a bacterium, not a mould, and was too toxic to use inside the body (Wikipedia, Pyocyanase; Molecules review PMC7916356). Mycophenolic acid (Gosio, 1893) came from a Penicillium mould but was never in wide clinical use as an antibacterial (Wikipedia, Bartolomeo Gosio). Salvarsan and the sulfonamides were made chemically, not by a mould (Science History Institute, Domagk). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyocyanase ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7916356 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomeo_Gosio

items.bron: NZ Electronic Text Centre, official history of New Zealand surgery in WWII: penicillin, introduced in the second half of 1943, gradually took over from the sulphonamides in treating wound infection. Sulfa drugs slowed bacterial growth, while penicillin killed bacteria and handled infections the sulfas could not. https://nzetc.victoria.ac.nz/tm/scholarly/tei-WH2Surg-pt1-c1-3.html

items.bron: This is an interpretation, not a stated fact. It follows from the confirmed sequence: Fleming's 1928 observation was not a usable medicine until the Oxford work of 1939-41 (Nature account; University of Oxford). The lesson does not claim Fleming was the first person ever to see a mould stop bacteria, which is just as well: others had reported it before him.

opsomming: Everything about Fleming, Oxford and the qualified 'first' superlative checks out, but the opening block says 'niks' could kill bacteria inside the body for most of history, which evidence contradicts (ancient tetracycline beer, Salvarsan, sulfa drugs, and the lesson's own 'ouer medisyne'), so the quantifier must be narrowed to 'no reliable medicine'; the lesson has no analogies to check.
